title: Ory's weekend club, consistent playing, and New Orleans way with tunes
summary: Ory ran the club two nights a week, played his crafted choruses the same each time with real vitality; Smith contrasts this with superficial modern trombonists and says New Orleans music is how you play any tune.

blocks.x: I would call it... He had a lot of sparkle. You know, there was a twinkle in those kiddish eyes of his. You know, and there was a lot of vitality in his movements. He used to wear him out. You know, we only played the two nights a week. It was his club, and he could call the shots as he wished. And business, I think, was such that he was wise. He stayed open on Friday and Saturday nights only. Didn't have to worry about bartender payrolls and all that sort of thing during the early part of the week when you would have died. And then the gamble is, do you make the money on the weekend or not? Well, he gambled, I'll stay open on the weekend only, and if we make it, we make it. You know, and it's a little more profit. I think that was probably good sound business. So we played the Friday and the Saturday nights. And by Saturday nights, he was pretty tired. Because he always gave. You know, he didn't hold back. He really played. Those choruses that you hear on the records, which I consider very carefully crafted works of musical art, they're his creations. I have no idea whether he worked them out in his head at some point in history, or if indeed he wrote them down at some point in history, memorized the concept, and then went with it. But he played his material just about the same every time. On a given tune, whether it be an oldie like Tiger Rag, or a simple basic old, old tune like Careless Love, or a fairly contemporary pop tune, or a hokum like Wabash Blues, things like that, which he'd play. Played it about the same. But he wasn't grinding it out in a perfunctory way. No, it was played, you know, with some guts. It really came from down. It had vitality. And at this point in time in 1975, I'm disappointed that none of the trombonists I've heard in New Orleans are playing with any kind of gut-level vitality. They're playing a little bit superficially. They're playing notes. They're playing notes. But playing jazz, the Laori conceived it. I was playing more than notes. You're playing a lot of raw emotion. And I like that. A lot of people can play Carnival of Venice and Flight of the Bumblebee. It's not very moving. Play a nice, simple, gutty chorus on something like Pagan Love Song. It can be a really nice musical experience. I think I learned in my first trip to New Orleans an important thing. In New Orleans music, it's not the name of the tune, but it's how you play any tune. Name me something off the hit parade. You know, that's saying, well, that dates me, doesn't it? Hit parade. But you just take something out of the pop milieu, and you play it in good, honest New Orleans style, then I think you've got an understanding of New Orleans music.
